title: Autoscale hysteresis and activation-delay worklog
content:
TL;DR:

This is a working log capturing the late-night incident on 2025-08-29 where Dedicated GPU pool latency spiked for ~27 minutes due to autoscale activation delay coupled with transient noisy-tenant allocations. The control loop that decides when to bring new VMs online has a 60s evaluation window plus a 90s VM provisioning guard (hysteresis). Under a pattern of many small bursts from a single noisy tenant we hit a corner case where the autoscaler repeatedly deferred provisioning because the short bursts didn’t exceed the per-eval threshold, but aggregate queueing exceeded the latency SLO. The net effect: repeated token-level timeouts and a cascade of client retries amplifying load until the autoscaler finally triggered and provisioned capacity.

Why this doc exists:
- capture timeline and signals for the incident review
- propose runbook and metrics changes to detect "hysteresis stall" earlier
- draft temporary mitigation (tunable threshold and emergency manual trigger)

Timeline (compacted):
- 2025-08-29 02:11 UTC: first latency alert from synthetic canaries (99p token latency > 350ms)
- 02:12 UTC: oncall page to SRE (Priya), initial Grafana shows bursty request arrival with short tails (10-35s spikes) from tenant: customer-omega-prod
- 02:13–02:20 UTC: autoscaler logs show repeated evaluate() events returning "no action" due to evaluate_window_max_rate check (configured min_concurrent_rps = 120)
- 02:18 UTC: engineer note: queue depth growing on existing nodes, per-model KV cache shows warm state, small seq lengths but high QPS per tenant
- 02:23 UTC: client-side retries start to increase (observed in trace logs), 02:26 UTC: two additional evaluation cycles finally decide to provision; VM pool adds 2 nodes by 02:34 UTC
- 02:38 UTC: latency returns to baseline, incident closes formally at 02:45 UTC after monitoring confirms stability

Observed signals and anomalies:
- Arrival pattern: many small concurrent streams (20–50 RPS each) from the same tenant rather than a single large request. The autoscaler’s rate estimator uses median-windowed metrics and misses short sharp increases that are correlated across many streams.
- Hysteresis guard: a 90s guard prevented back-to-back provisioning in some cases; combined with 60s evaluation windows this allowed a ~3-minute effective delay where repeated partial increases didn’t cross the provisioning threshold.
- Noisy neighbor amplification: the tenant used many ephemeral sessions causing inefficient packing and KV cache fragmentation. This raised per-token compute overhead (more context switches and scheduling jitter).
- Telemetry gap: we lacked a single-rollup metric that combines queue depth + pending_requests_at_priority which would have shown a clear capacity deficit earlier.

Hypothesis (root cause):
Primary: Autoscaler decision logic is overly conservative for bursty-multiplexed workloads from a single tenant; the combination of median-window smoothing and hysteresis guard allowed sustained underprovisioning.
Secondary: Tenant-specific allocation pattern (many short-lived streams) resulted in suboptimal packing and additional per-request cost (KV cache churn). This made the same compute footprint more expensive and drove actual utilization above what the autoscaler predicted.

Immediate mitigations applied during incident:
- Manual emergency provision via infra self-service: added 2 nodes (02:26–02:34) to relieve queue backlog.
- Rate limit knob applied to offending tenant at edge (temporary throttle to 200 RPS aggregate) to stop retry amplification while capacity came up.
- Post-incident: tenant outreach scheduled to discuss request shaping and recommended client-side QPS guidelines.

Proposed runbook changes (draft):
1) Detect "hysteresis stall" pattern:
   - New composite alert: if evaluation returns N consecutive "no action" but queue_depth_in_tokens > Q and pending_request_latency > L for > 45s, fire high-priority alert.
   - Practical thresholds: Q = 250k token-equivalent queue, L = 200ms 95p response increase. (Needs tuning.)
2) Add a short-circuit emergency provision path in autoscaler:
   - If composite alert flips to true, bypass hysteresis guards and provision a small incremental unit (1 node or fractional GPU) immediately.
3) Tenant-level signals and isolation:
   - Track tenant-local packing efficiency metric (avg_active_sessions_per_gpu and kv_cache_miss_rate). If packing efficiency drops below 0.65, schedule isolation and/or burst-capacity gating.
4) Instrumentation additions:
   - New metric: pending_token_equivalent_by_tenant (compute queue depth weighted by expected per-token cost)
   - New tracing tag: autoscale-decision-reason on provisioning traces to correlate human actions with decision loops.

Playbook steps for oncall (draft):
- P0 latency alert -> check synthetic canary + cluster-wide queue depth dashboard -> if high queue but autoscaler returning no action, escalate to SRE ops and follow "hysteresis stall" checklist:
  1. Check autoscaler logs: how many consecutive no-action cycles? timestamp each evaluate() result.
  2. Query pending_token_equivalent_by_tenant for top-5 tenants. If top tenant >= Q threshold, apply emergency throttle and page tenant-owner.
  3. If manual provision allowed: use infra self-service to add minimal incremental capacity; avoid over-provisioning that exacerbates packing.
  4. Monitor client retry rates; if retries amplify, consider temporary 429 gateway policy with short TTL.
  5. After capacity added, watch KV cache warm-up (per-model KV hit rate) and rollback temp throttles.

Longer-term engineering actions (owners and rough timelines):
- Autoscaler policy change to include short-window burst detector (Eng-serving-runtime) — owner: Jon Park — plan Q4 2025 prototype
- New tenant packing telemetry and UI surfaces in Console (Product + Devexp) — owner: Marta Li — plan Q1 2026
- Introduce fractional GPU provisioning experiment (hybrid packs) to mitigate 3–5 node provisioning delays for small bursts (Infra) — owner: Ethan Rivera — feasibility spike 3 weeks

Experiment ideas to validate hypothesis:
- Replay the exact arrival pattern in the autoscale simulator (use the August-29 request trace) and compare decision paths with and without median smoothing.
- A/B test lowering hysteresis from 90s -> 30s in a canary pool to observe false-positive provision rate vs latency reduction.

Open questions and uncertainties:
- What exact tenant behaviors caused KV cache fragmentation? client library patterns? short-lived sessions? (Need tenant logs and SDK versions.)
- Are we comfortable bypassing hysteresis in certain emergency cases without opening ourselves to oscillation? need simulation evidence.
- How much of the increased per-token cost is due to scheduling jitter vs pure compute saturation? collect host-level perf counters on next repro.

Action items (short list):
- [ ] Add composite alert to Grafana (Priya) — due 2025-09-09
- [ ] Run autoscaler replay for 2025-08-29 trace and commit result to runtime repo (Jon) — due 2025-09-16
- [ ] Start tenant outreach for customer-omega-prod (CSSE + Solutions) — Marta to coordinate — due 2025-09-05
- [ ] Prototype emergency provision short-circuit in staging (Ethan) — due 2025-10-01

Notes to self / oncall anecdotes:
- Late-night paging fatigue made the manual provision decision slower; consider lowering friction for emergency manual add (pre-authorized scripts).
- The tracer correlation between gateway retries and autoscaler decisions was crucial — invest in making that an automatic panel in the P0 view.

Appendix: quick log excerpts (sanitized):
- autoscaler.log 02:14:11 evaluate window=60s median_rps=88 target_min=120 => no_action (smoothing)
- queue-metrics 02:20:03 pending_tokens=312412 top_tenant=customer-omega-prod
- gateway-traces 02:25:22 retry-rate-top=customer-omega-prod count=540/min

If reviewing: please comment inline on proposed thresholds (Q/L) and whether emergency bypass is acceptable as a short-term safety valve.

End of worklog.
